sections.h2: Which route fits a Pontiac house?
sections.html:
Owners in Pontiac can list with an agent, sell on their own, or take an offer from a company that buys houses directly. The city is the Oakland County seat, which puts the deed office and the treasurer, who handle recording for every sale, nearby.

Usually the condition of the house picks the route. A sound property with clean permit records suits a public listing. A property with deferred repairs, an occupant, tax trouble or an inherited title often moves faster with a buyer who takes it as it stands. Whichever way you go, put terms on paper and have a closing agent check ownership and any recorded liens.

Pontiac sits between Auburn Hills, Waterford Township and Bloomfield Township, and older houses near downtown, including the Fairgrove Avenue Historic District, date from the auto-industry boom of the 1910s and 1920s. Housing is modestly priced. For 2020 to 2024 the middle owner-occupied value was $121,700 and the middle rent was $1,063. Owners occupy 46.6% of the housing, so a large part of the stock is rented.

The July 1, 2025 estimate is 62,077 residents, up 0.8% from the April 2020 base. The city has 25,617 households averaging 2.36 people, with a middle income of $44,329. Owners with a mortgage pay about $1,223 a month at the middle of the range.

Modest prices and plenty of renters mean small investors shop for Pontiac houses alongside people planning to live in them. A buyer with cash can skip the lender-driven repair demands that often come with older houses. Out-of-area buyers also ask which school serves the address, so confirm with the district before you list.

Snowfall averages 36.0 inches a year in Pontiac and the record low is minus 22 F. A cold, empty house puts pipes, roof and furnace under strain. If yours sits vacant, leave the heat running all winter and get the roof and gutters looked at before anyone tours it.

Pontiac planning handles three applications worth knowing: Zoning Board of Appeals, Historic District Approval and Zoning Compliance. Exterior changes to a house in the Fairgrove Avenue district or any other historic area may need approval first, and a buyer with renovation plans will want to know what the rules permit.

The State of Michigan, not the city, permits curb cuts and driveways on state roads like Woodward and Telegraph. Changed a driveway on a lot that touches one? Keep that paperwork with your records. Oakland County's Water Resources Commission runs soil erosion control inside Pontiac, which matters for a vacant lot or a house with grading work underway. For anything else, ask Pontiac planning staff what applies to the parcel.

sections.h2: Selling a rental house in Pontiac
sections.html:
The city code requires owners of one- and two-family dwellings occupied by someone other than the owner to register them with the Department of Building Safety. A new owner re-registers within 60 days after a change of ownership.

Pontiac rental registry rules
SituationWhat the code requires
Late registration$25.00 fee per rental unit per month
Routine inspectionAt intervals of no more than three years
Vacated unitInspection before anyone moves back in, and the owner tells Building Safety first
Occupying before a certificate of complianceMunicipal civil infraction, $500.00 fine, each day a separate offense
Recorded land contract naming the occupantExempt from the registry

Own a house with tenants? Call Building Safety about the certificate status before you sell. Whoever buys it to keep renting must register within 60 days.

Pontiac's city hall does not record deeds. Oakland County does, after its staff look over each document and accept those that meet the statutory rules. A deed costs $30.00 to record, and a warranty deed needs a treasurer's tax certificate first, at $5.00.

The county taxes transfers where the consideration is above $99.99. Redemption payments on Sheriff Deed and Clerk Deed foreclosures also go through this office, and only someone with an interest in the property can make one. An owner facing a foreclosure sale should get the payoff figure before choosing a buyer.

Copies of recorded documents are available from the county, and its index starts at January 1, 1964. Inherited the house? Pull the chain of title early so a missing paper cannot stall closing.

Among the city's income tax forms is a Request for Income Tax Compliance Clearance. Ask the Pontiac income tax office if your sale needs one.

Once an offer is accepted, the closing agent searches title and recorded liens. A tenant in the house means a check with Building Safety on registration and certificate status. Foreclosure in play? Ask the county for the payoff first. Inherited? Collect the recorded documents so the chain of title is whole.

At closing the deed is signed and recorded, tax certification is handled for a warranty deed, and the transfer tax is paid. Keep copies of every permit, approval and registration record for the buyer. A cash buyer can often close faster because no lender is waiting on an appraisal or inspection report.

Two situations call for extra lead time in Pontiac. With an inherited house, the title has to be traced through every recorded transfer, and any missing document needs to be found before a buyer's title company asks. Allow time for that search, because a gap can pause a closing for weeks.

With a looming foreclosure, the redemption payoff comes from the Oakland County deed office, and only a person with an interest in the property may redeem. Get the number in writing, compare it with what each buyer offers, and choose the buyer whose closing date lands ahead of any deadline. A buyer paying cash can often meet a tight date because no lender is involved.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
Collect your deed, the latest tax bill and any permits for a roof, furnace or addition. If the house is a rental, add the registration record, the certificate of compliance and the tenant's lease. If the lot touches Woodward or Telegraph and you changed the driveway, include the state permit. A folder with these items answers most of the questions a buyer or title company will ask.

Call Building Safety, the planning office and the income tax office with your address in hand, and write down what each one tells you. That short list becomes your checklist for closing day.

faqs.q: Can a Pontiac house with tenants be sold?
faqs.a: Yes, but registration and inspection rules apply. Pontiac requires one- and two-family rentals to be registered with Building Safety and inspected at least every three years, and a buyer must re-register within 60 days of the ownership change.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for occupying a Pontiac rental before inspection?
faqs.a: The ordinance sets a $500.00 municipal civil infraction fine, and each day is a separate offense. The owner or agent must notify Building Safety before a vacated unit is reoccupied.

faqs.q: Which office files a deed for a Pontiac property?
faqs.a: The Oakland County Register of Deeds. A warranty deed needs a treasurer's tax certificate at a $5.00 fee first, and a deed recording costs $30.00.

faqs.q: Does heavy snow matter when selling in Pontiac?
faqs.a: Pontiac averages 36.0 inches of snow a year. Roof condition, gutters and a working furnace matter most, and an empty house needs steady heat so pipes do not freeze before the buyer's inspection.

faqs.q: What is the middle home value in Pontiac?
faqs.a: $121,700 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. That is a citywide figure, so compare recent sales on your own block before accepting an offer.
